title: Save with purpose: goals, safe places and your emergency fund

say: Save with purpose: goals, safe places, and your emergency fund.
This is the video for Module 2, Saving Money: Building Your Safety Net and Future.
Saving means keeping part of today's money for tomorrow. The secret is to give your savings a clear job. Money with a job is much easier to protect.
The first job is to protect the family from shocks, like illness or a broken shop freezer.

panel.heading: Give your savings a job
items: Reach goals bigger than one month's income

say: The second is to reach goals that cost more than one month's income, like rent or a sewing machine.

panel.heading: Give your savings a job
items: Reach goals bigger than one month's income

say: The third is to seize opportunities, like buying stock in bulk at a good price, without borrowing.

panel.heading: Give your savings a job

say: A real goal has an amount, a purpose and a date. For example, Kemi sells provisions in Abeokuta and wants a deep freezer costing about 300,000 naira. She sets a date 10 months away.

panel.heading: Work backwards from a goal
items: Cuts take-away lunch, buys stock in bulk

say: 300,000 divided by 10 months is about 30,000 naira a month.

panel.heading: Work backwards from a goal

say: That is about 7,000 naira a week.

panel.heading: Work backwards from a goal
items: Cuts take-away lunch, buys stock in bulk

say: She already saves 3,000 a week, so she needs about 4,000 more.

panel.heading: Work backwards from a goal
items: Cuts take-away lunch, buys stock in bulk

say: From her tracking she cuts daily take-away lunch and buys shop stock in larger, cheaper quantities.
Most people save what is left at month end, and usually nothing is left. So pay yourself first. Move your savings out the moment money arrives, ideally by automatic transfer.

panel.rule: Save first, the moment money comes in. Spend after.

say: Choose where to save by the job of the money. Safety first, access second, returns third.
Before you save anywhere, check these five things. If any answer is no or unclear, do not put your savings there. Money in an unlicensed scheme has no NDIC protection.
And keep savings in a separate account from your spending, with no debit card attached.

Women have saved together for generations, in ajo, esusu, adashe and isusu. For example, ten market women in Ibadan each pay about 20,000 naira a month for ten months. Each month one woman collects about 200,000 naira.
But there are real risks. The collector can disappear with members' money.

panel.heading: Saving with others: the real risks

cards.d: Usually no insurance, and recovering the money is difficult.
A member stops paying after collecting, so later members receive less or nothing.
Disputes about who paid what. Keep a signed record book at every meeting.

say: A member can stop paying after collecting. Bisi drew number 2 and collected in month 2, but she must keep paying until month 10.

say: And poor records lead to disputes. Write the rules down, sign the record book at every meeting, and where possible keep group money in an account that needs two signatories.

say: Join only groups of people you know well and can find. In a real ajo, every member pays in and receives the same amount, with written rules and records.

panel.heading: Real ajo or a ponzi scheme?
left: People you know and can find
Everyone gets back what they paid
right: Promises more than you put in
Must recruit others to get paid

say: Be very careful with anyone promising high guaranteed returns, or paying you to bring in new members.
Or asking you to pay into a personal account, or pressuring you to act fast. That is a ponzi scheme, not ajo.
And licensed banks never ask for your PIN, password or OTP.

say: An emergency fund is money kept only for real, unexpected problems, like sudden illness or losing your main customer. Rent and school fees are not emergencies. They get their own pots.
Aim for three to six months of essential expenses. For example, Amaka is a single mother in Enugu.
Her food costs about 60,000 naira a month, her rent share 25,000, and transport 15,000.
Her children's school costs are 15,000, and electricity, water, medicine and toiletries come to about 15,000.
So her essentials are about 130,000 naira a month. That is her starter target. Three months would be about 390,000.
She saves about 15,000 a month in a separate account, and adds any extra income to speed it up.
When an emergency happens, pause and confirm it is truly unplanned and necessary.

say: Take only what you need, keep the receipt, and write down how much you took out.

say: Then restart saving the next month. Using the fund is not failure. It is exactly what it is for. The only mistake is not rebuilding it.
